0.alt: Glútty: More safety and confidence for people with celiac disease when eating out
2.text: Celiac disease is an autoimmune condition triggered by the ingestion of gluten — a protein found in wheat, barley, rye and their derivatives — that can cause inflammation in the small intestine and impair the body’s absorption of essential nutrients. Mayo Clinic — Celiac Disease Overview
3.text: International studies indicate that celiac disease affects approximately 1% of the world’s population, with diagnoses growing steadily over recent decades. Systematic reviews show that the prevalence of the disease has increased significantly in recent years, both in European countries and in other regions of the world. Celiac Disease Foundation — Global Prevalence Study
4.text: In Brazil, although there are still limitations related to diagnosis and underreporting of cases, studies point to prevalence rates similar to those observed in European populations, showing that celiac disease is also a relevant challenge in the Brazilian food context. PubMed Central — Celiac Disease in Brazilian Patients
5.text: Despite growing awareness of gluten-free eating, there are still important gaps in the experience of people with celiac disease when eating out.
6.text: Issues related to trust in the available information, the risk of cross-contamination and the difficulty of validating the safety of establishments began to appear repeatedly during the early stages of the investigation.
7.text: This context raised a central question for the development of the project:
8.text: How could digital experiences support people with celiac disease when making food decisions away from home?
11.text: People with celiac disease live every day with the need to avoid any contact with gluten so as not to suffer significant health impacts. When eating out, this need turns an everyday activity into a process often marked by insecurity, fear of cross-contamination and difficulty trusting the available information.
13.text: Men and women who follow a gluten-free diet and constantly need to make food decisions without clear, standardized or reliable information about the safety of establishments.
15.text: The difficulty of finding places that are truly considered safe directly affects these people’s autonomy, social life and quality of life.
16.text: Beyond the dietary limitation, there is also a continuous effort to validate information, reduce risks and avoid negative experiences related to cross-contamination.
18.text: Today, many people with celiac disease still struggle to identify trustworthy establishments, understand how food is prepared and assess the level of safety offered by restaurants.
19.text: The lack of standardized information and community validation mechanisms increases insecurity throughout the entire food decision-making process.
20.text: More than finding restaurants with gluten-free options, people with celiac disease often need to interpret signs of trust, reduce uncertainty and validate information before even having a meal.
21.text: Based on this need, a strategic stage began, focused on analyzing the market, identifying opportunities and initially structuring the digital solution.
24.text: With a clearer understanding of the problem and the context faced by people with celiac disease when eating out, the next stage of the project sought to understand how the market currently responds to these needs and what opportunities existed to build a safer, more transparent and more trustworthy experience.
25.text: More than analyzing isolated features, this phase aimed to understand how factors related to trust, clarity of information and decision-making influenced the experience of people with celiac disease when looking for gluten-free restaurants and products.
26.text: To support this strategic analysis, different UX Strategy techniques and frameworks were used, including goal setting through the SMART methodology, benchmarking of digital solutions, benchmarking of establishments offering gluten-free food, the Value Proposition Canvas, the Business Model Canvas and the AARRR framework to structure initial hypotheses on acquisition, retention and growth of the platform.
27.text: During the studies, it became clear that the problem was not only the lack of gluten-free options, but mainly the difficulty of validating information, understanding preparation processes and trusting the safety of establishments.
28.text: Based on what was learned during this strategic stage, there was a need to turn the project’s main directions into clearer, more structured objectives.
29.text: To do so, the SMART methodology was used, making it possible to define specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound goals to guide the first stages of development and validation of the solution.
32.text: To begin the strategic direction of the project, a competitive benchmarking was carried out to understand how different digital solutions and specialized establishments dealt with food safety, trust and communication about dietary restrictions.
34.text: Apps such as Find Me Gluten Free, HappyCow and FoodisGood were analyzed, as well as restaurants, cafés and supermarkets offering gluten-free food in Switzerland.
36.text: The study revealed that many solutions already offered important features, such as collaborative reviews, dietary filters and ingredient information, but still had limitations in the clarity of their communication and in building trust for people with celiac disease.
37.text: The main learnings showed that transparency, community reviews, clarity about cross-contamination and a personalized experience were essential factors for reducing insecurity and supporting safer food decisions.
39.text: Based on the patterns identified during the analyses, Glútty’s initial value proposition was structured.
40.text: The goal of this stage was to understand in more depth:
41.text: The pains; needs; expectations; and desired gains of people with dietary restrictions.
43.text: During the strategic stage, the studies helped broaden the understanding of the challenges faced by people with celiac disease when eating out. Beyond finding gluten-free options, issues began to emerge related to the transparency of information, the difficulty of validating ingredients, insecurity about preparation processes and a constant fear of cross-contamination.
44.text: The analyses also revealed impacts that went beyond the functional dimension of eating, including a sense of social limitation, difficulty maintaining a balanced eating routine and a continuous effort to find establishments considered truly trustworthy.
45.text: Beyond the need for food safety, opportunities related to convenience and autonomy during decision-making began to appear. Features such as personalized filters, community reviews, detailed ingredient information and recommendations based on eating habits emerged as possible ways to make the experience clearer and more predictable for users.
46.text: Another important learning from this stage was understanding the value of sharing experiences among people with celiac disease. Being able to access reports, reviews and information shared by other users appeared as a relevant factor in increasing the perception of trust when choosing gluten-free restaurants and products.
48.text: During the strategic stage, the Business Model Canvas helped structure not only possible operating models for the solution, but also understand which elements would be needed to sustain a more trustworthy, accessible and relevant experience for people with dietary restrictions.
50.text: During the strategic stage, the Business Model Canvas helped structure not only possible operating models for the solution, but also understand which elements would be needed to sustain a more trustworthy, accessible and relevant experience for people with dietary restrictions.
51.text: The analyses showed that Glútty’s value proposition would not be limited to discovering gluten-free restaurants, but would also involve creating a more personalized, practical and safe experience throughout the entire food journey. Elements such as contextual recommendations, transparency about ingredients and preparation processes, community reviews and decision-making support began to emerge as important parts of the experience.
52.text: The canvas also helped identify different user profiles with distinct needs, including recently diagnosed people, users with severe intolerance, parents of children with celiac disease and consumers with multiple dietary restrictions. This segmentation reinforced the need to build a flexible experience that adapts to different contexts of use.
53.text: Another important learning from this stage was understanding the role of community, a welcoming attitude and personalization as relevant factors in the relationship with users. Features related to sharing experiences, shared reviews, loyalty programs and personalized recommendations appeared as possible ways to strengthen engagement and recurring use within the platform.
54.text: Beyond the user experience, the Business Model Canvas also helped visualize possible strategic partnerships involving restaurants, health professionals, digital influencers, celiac communities and delivery platforms, broadening the view of the ecosystem needed to sustain the growth of the solution over time.
56.text: During the strategic stage, the AARRR framework helped structure possible paths related to the acquisition, activation, retention, referral and revenue of the solution, broadening the view of how the experience could evolve beyond the initial use of the platform.
58.text: The analyses showed that growth strategies for Glútty would be strongly connected to building trust and to the presence of the community throughout the user journey. Partnerships with specialized restaurants, educational content about safe eating and participation in digital communities emerged as possible forms of acquisition aligned with the context of the celiac audience.
59.text: In the activation stage, opportunities began to appear related to reducing insecurity during the first contact with the platform. Elements such as a welcoming onboarding, intuitive filters, visual food-safety markers and highlighted community reviews emerged as important features to support users during their first interactions with the product.
60.text: The studies also revealed possibilities related to retention and continuous engagement, including personalized recommendations, alerts about new safe restaurants, relevant content and gamification mechanisms aimed at community participation.
61.text: In addition, the framework helped explore forms of organic referral and growth based on experiences shared among users, through referral systems, sharing of reviews and highlighting real stories within the platform and on social media.
62.text: Another important learning from this stage was understanding that possible monetization strategies would need to stay aligned with the solution’s value proposition, prioritizing useful and relevant experiences for users, such as premium features, partnerships with establishments and content related to the world of gluten-free eating.
63.text: The UX Strategy stage was essential for turning initial perceptions into more concrete directions for the product.
64.text: The studies showed that people with celiac disease are not just looking for gluten-free restaurants, but for experiences that convey clarity, predictability and trust during food decision-making.
65.text: Based on these learnings, Glútty began to be structured as a solution focused not only on discovering places, but also on food transparency, a personalized experience and building collective safety through the community.
67.text: During the strategic stage, the CSD matrix (Certainties, Suppositions and Doubts) was used to organize initial perceptions, behavioral hypotheses and questions that would still need to be validated throughout the project.
69.text: Building the matrix helped consolidate some patterns already identified during the initial analyses, mainly related to the difficulty of finding trustworthy establishments, the insecurity caused by cross-contamination and the need for clearer information about ingredients, preparation and food safety.
70.text: The discussions also reinforced the role of the community in food decision-making. Sharing experiences among people with celiac disease appeared as one of the main sources of trust when choosing gluten-free restaurants and products, highlighting the value of shared reviews within the experience proposed by the platform.
71.text: Beyond the certainties already identified, the matrix also made it possible to structure hypotheses about user behavior, including the possibility that detailed information about preparation and cross-contamination risks would increase the perception of safety when using the platform. Suppositions also emerged about the impact of perceived trust in community reviews when choosing where to eat.
72.text: Another important point of this stage was identifying doubts that would still need to be investigated in the next phases of the project, including which information would be truly essential to support users’ decision-making, to what extent community reviews would be enough to build trust and how to present complex content clearly and objectively within the interface.
74.text: At the end of this stage, the strategic directions helped build a broader understanding of the challenges faced by people with celiac disease when eating out, revealing that the problem was not only related to the availability of gluten-free options, but also to the difficulty of trusting the available information, understanding preparation processes and reducing insecurity during food decision-making.
75.text: The analyses carried out throughout this phase also revealed factors related to autonomy, convenience, a welcoming attitude, socializing and personalization of the experience, showing how different emotional, informational and behavioral aspects influenced users’ relationship with eating out.
76.text: Besides identifying opportunities related to transparency of information, community participation and building trust, this stage also helped raise important hypotheses that would still need to be explored in the next phases of the project.
77.text: Questions related to the perception of safety, the impact of shared reviews, the criteria users apply to validate establishments, information needs during food choices and different behaviors in the face of cross-contamination risk began to emerge as relevant topics for investigation.
78.text: These learnings served as the basis for directing the next stages of the project, including UX Research, MVP definition, information architecture and the development of the first flows of the experience.
79.text: UX Strategy: Initial strategic direction to connect people with celiac disease to safe restaurants
80.text: UX Research - Investigating fear, trust and eating behavior.
81.text: After the UX Strategy stage, I structured a mixed-methods study to understand how fear, trust and validation influence the decision-making of people with celiac disease when eating out. The investigation combined a quantitative survey with 86 valid responses and 7 semi-structured qualitative interviews, making it possible to cross behavioral patterns with motivations, emotions and contexts of use.
82.text: In the quantitative stage, consistent signs of food insecurity and a search for validation emerged: 88% said they rely on recommendations from other people with celiac disease when looking for restaurants considered safe; 66% pointed to cross-contamination as their main concern; 93% had already felt uncomfortable or embarrassed explaining their dietary restriction in restaurants; and 58% said they trust only a few restaurants that claim to have gluten-free options.
83.text: The qualitative stage deepened these patterns and showed that eating out is no longer a spontaneous decision: it now requires planning, constant checking and adaptation strategies. By crossing the quantitative and qualitative findings, it became clear that safe eating does not depend only on gluten-free options existing, but on building trust throughout the entire journey. These learnings guided decisions related to Glútty’s information architecture, community validation, personalized experience and communication.
85.text: The questionnaire was structured to investigate: how often people eat out; risk perception; trust criteria; negative experiences; emotional impact; validation habits.
86.text: In total, 86 people answered the survey.
87.text: The data revealed recurring patterns related to trust, insecurity and decision-making:
88.items.0: 88% said they rely on recommendations from other people with celiac disease when looking for restaurants considered safe;
92.items.0: 93% of participants reported having felt uncomfortable or embarrassed explaining their dietary restriction in restaurants, either frequently or occasionally.
94.items.0: 58% said they trust only a few restaurants that claim to have gluten-free options.
96.text: These numbers showed that the challenges of gluten-free eating went beyond purely dietary issues, also involving emotional, social and behavioral impacts.
98.text: The interviews showed that eating out requires constant planning, research in advance and adaptation strategies. Many participants reported avoiding unfamiliar restaurants, going back to places they had already tested or bringing their own food to reduce risks and insecurity.
99.text: The accounts also revealed a direct impact on autonomy, routine and social life, as well as a recurring fear of getting sick and the influence of previous contamination experiences on the perception of safety.
100.text: Even in places considered safe, many participants still showed fear and vigilance during the meal.
101.text: This finding reinforced a central point of the research:
102.text: The emotional journey doesn’t end when the dish arrives at the table.
103.text: Beyond emotional insecurity, the accounts also revealed a constant cognitive effort during food decision-making.
104.text: Participants described the ongoing need to: validate information; look up recommendations; interpret signs of safety; analyze ingredients; and monitor possible risks of cross-contamination.
105.text: These behaviors showed that food decision-making involves multiple stages of validation, comparison and risk reduction before the meal even happens.
106.text:
The learnings from the research began to directly guide decisions related to information architecture, personalization criteria, community reviews and the ways information is presented within the product experience.
These learnings helped turn abstract perceptions into concrete directions for the product, influencing decisions related to information architecture, community validation mechanisms, personalization of the experience and communication strategies aimed at building trust.
107.text: This section presents only a summary of the main learnings. The complete process of research, interviews, analyses and artifacts can be found in the detailed UX Research case.
108.text: UX Research — The user research process in practice
109.text: Personas and User Journey - Turning behaviors into design opportunities
111.text: Based on the patterns identified during the interviews, behavioral personas were built to represent the different profiles, needs and strategies adopted by people with celiac disease when eating out.
112.text: More than demographic profiles, the personas synthesize the behaviors, insecurities, motivations and decision-making processes observed throughout the research.
113.text: These profiles helped turn the research findings into concrete product directions, keeping the focus on the real pains and contexts experienced by the participants.
115.text: Michelle represents users who deal every day with the need to balance routine, social life and food safety.
116.text: Her behavior highlighted the importance of features focused on: community validation; transparency of information; reducing uncertainty; and supporting decision-making when choosing restaurants.
118.text: Based on the personas and the patterns identified during the research, a user journey map was developed to understand how people with celiac disease experience the process of deciding where to eat out.
119.text: The analysis revealed that this decision involves multiple stages of validation, comparison and search for safety, going far beyond simply choosing a restaurant.
121.text: Throughout the journey, recurring moments of: anxiety; insecurity; constant vigilance; and high cognitive effort were identified.
122.text: The greatest tensions appeared mainly during: the validation of information; the interaction with the restaurant; and the moment of eating the meal.
124.text: The mapping showed that safe eating does not depend only on gluten-free options existing, but also on the sense of trust built throughout the entire experience.
125.text: These learnings helped guide design decisions focused on reducing uncertainty, increasing transparency and emotionally supporting the user throughout the entire food journey.
126.text: This section presents a summary of the main personas and learnings from the user journey. The complete analysis can be found in the detailed Personas and User Journey case.

129.text: How the experience was structured to support safer food decisions
130.text: The solution architecture was built on the behavioral and emotional patterns identified during the user research.
131.text: More than organizing features or structuring screens, the goal was to create an experience capable of continuously supporting the user before, during and after the meal.
132.text: The research revealed that the decision to eat out involves insecurity, constant validation, cognitive effort and an ongoing need for confirmation.
133.caption: Answer taken from the user interviews.
134.text: That is why the product architecture was designed to turn multiple moments of anxiety into a more predictable, contextualized and trustworthy experience.
135.text: The architecture was designed to reduce emotional friction and lower the effort needed to make safer food decisions.
136.text: How the user journey shaped the structure of the experience
137.text: When analyzing the participants’ behaviors, it became clear that the eating experience did not happen in isolation.
138.text: Users constantly went through cycles of: research;comparison;validation;decision;consumption;and re-evaluation of the experience.
139.text: For this reason, the architecture was structured as a continuous decision-support flow, connecting each stage of the journey instead of treating features as separate tasks.
140.text: Each journey represents a different emotional and behavioral moment of the eating experience, requiring specific needs for support, validation and safety.

142.text: How the flows were organized along the journey
143.text: The journeys were organized to follow real behaviors observed during the research.
144.text: Each stage was designed to respond to specific needs identified throughout the user experience:
145.text:
onboarding and personalization to reduce future effort;
search and review to increase trust;
preparation before going out to reduce anxiety;
eating the meal to reinforce the sense of safety;
and the post-experience to strengthen sharing and community validation.
146.text: The Home as the center of the experience
147.text: Another important direction was to turn the Home into the main hub of the experience.
148.text: Instead of fragmenting features into multiple complex paths, navigation was structured to centralize discovery, review, decision and sharing in a predictable, continuous flow.
149.text: This decision helped reduce cognitive overload and made it easier to quickly access the most important information during food decision-making.
150.text: The structure of the solution was organized to connect discovery, validation, decision and sharing in a single experience flow.

152.text: The role of the community in building trust
153.text: One of the central principles of the architecture was to make the community an active part of the experience.
154.text: The reviews and reports shared by users continuously feed the system, strengthening collective trust and helping other people in future food decisions.
155.text: This cycle turns individual experiences into shared intelligence, allowing the platform to evolve continuously from the contributions of the community itself.
156.text: How research insights shaped the architecture
157.text: Several architectural decisions came directly from the behaviors identified during the research.
158.text: The constant need for validation led to the creation of detailed reviews and levels of perceived safety.
159.text: The cognitive effort involved in searching for information led to centralizing data on preparation, ingredients and cross-contamination.
160.text: And the fear of constantly repeating explanations led to the creation of a customizable food profile, making it possible to adapt the experience to the user’s restrictions and preferences.
162.text: The solution architecture stopped focusing only on searching for gluten-free restaurants and began to structure the entire food decision experience in an integrated way.
163.text: Each flow was designed to reduce insecurity, support the user emotionally and make trust a central part of the experience.
164.text: More than connecting features, the architecture began to structure relationships of trust throughout the entire user experience.
165.text: This section presents a summary of the product’s main architectural directions. The complete process of defining the flows, organizing the experience and making structural decisions can be found in the detailed Solution Architecture case.
166.text: Solution architecture: connecting journeys in a continuous flow
168.text: After the UX Research stage, it became clear that Glútty’s main challenge was not just helping people with celiac disease find gluten-free restaurants, but supporting a decision journey marked by insecurity, constant validation and fear of cross-contamination.
169.text: The research showed that, before choosing where to eat, users need to check information, compare options, interpret signs of safety and rely on experiences shared by other people with similar restrictions. That is why the MVP definition started from a central question:
170.text: Which features are truly essential to reduce insecurity and support safer food decisions from the very first version of the product?
171.text: To answer this question, the features identified during the previous stages were organized and assessed according to two main criteria: impact for the user and implementation effort.
172.text: This prioritization helped prevent the initial product from becoming too broad, too complex or disconnected from the most urgent pains identified in the research.
174.text: The impact and effort matrix made it possible to distinguish features essential for the MVP from features that could be developed in later phases. The initial focus was to prioritize solutions capable of delivering immediate value with less complexity, especially those related to personalization, search, filters, validation of information and community reviews.
175.text: Based on this analysis, the MVP was structured around a minimum food decision-support flow:
178.text: This organization helped turn isolated features into a continuous journey. The user starts by personalizing their experience, finds options compatible with their restrictions, validates important information before deciding and reuses experiences considered safe on future occasions.
179.text: In practice, this flow was broken down into more specific steps:
181.text: The initial MVP scope came to include: onboarding with a safety standard, search by location, filters by restriction, recommendations by profile and community validation, restaurant and dish details, information on ingredients, risks and safety level, structured feedback with tags, as well as favorites, history and notifications.
182.text: These features were prioritized because they respond directly to the main research learnings: reducing search effort, making critical information more visible, supporting safety validation and turning community experiences into useful signals for other users.
183.text: At the same time, some features were left for future phases, such as more advanced social features, gamification, a rewards system, bookings, delivery and more complex verification mechanisms. These ideas remain relevant, but require more technical and operational effort or additional validation before being added to the product.
185.text: The roadmap helped organize this evolution more strategically, separating what should be validated first in the MVP from what could expand the value of the solution in later phases.
186.text: This decision reinforced an important principle of the project: before expanding Glútty into a more complete platform, it was necessary to validate the core of the experience — helping people with celiac disease find, assess and choose places with more clarity, trust and predictability.
187.text: In this way, the MVP definition was not treated as a list of features, but as a strategic product decision. The goal was to build a lean first version, consistent with the research data and capable of testing Glútty’s core proposition: supporting safer food decisions through personalization, transparency and community validation.
188.text: This section presents a summary of the main learnings related to the MVP definition and feature prioritization. The complete process, including the impact and effort matrix, feature analysis and evolution roadmap, can be found in the detailed MVP and prioritization case.

191.text: With the main flows of the solution already defined in the previous stages, the next phase of the project sought to turn the strategic directions and research insights into initial interface structures.
192.text: More than exploring visual aesthetics, the goal of this stage was to organize flows, hierarchies and relationships between features, making it possible to visualize how the user experience could work continuously throughout the food journey.
193.text: The low-fidelity wireframes helped explore navigation possibilities, distribution of information, content prioritization and the first behaviors of the interface before visual refinement began.
197.text: The first explorations were initially done on paper through quick sketches, making it possible to test ideas more freely and iteratively before building the flows digitally.
198.text: This approach helped speed up decisions related to information architecture, placement of features and continuity between different stages of the experience.
199.text: During this process, explorations emerged related to:
200.text: onboarding and personalization; restaurant search; dietary filters; viewing dishes; validation mechanisms; structured reviews; favorites; and food profile.
201.text: More than defining isolated screens, this stage helped understand how different features could connect within a more continuous and predictable journey for the user.
204.text: The wireframes also helped validate how critical food-safety information would be distributed throughout the experience.
205.text: During the explorations, it became clear that information related to ingredients, risks, community reviews and safety criteria needed to appear progressively and in context — avoiding cognitive overload during navigation.
206.text: This stage was important to structure:
207.text: information hierarchies; decision points; continuity between screens; navigation patterns; and mechanisms for personalizing the experience.

210.text: The stage also reinforced the importance of:
211.text: reducing cognitive effort; making critical information more accessible; supporting food decisions progressively; and building a more predictable experience for users who live with constant food insecurity.

216.text: UX Writing — communication as decision support
217.text: With the main flows of the experience already structured in the previous stages, the next phase of the project sought to explore how the interface’s communication could reduce insecurity and support food decisions in a clearer, more human and more predictable way.
218.text: In the context of gluten-free eating, the research showed that the problem was not only the lack of information, but also the difficulty of trusting it. Many people reported anxiety when reading menus, insecurity about cross-contamination risks and fear of making the wrong decisions when eating out.
219.text: Based on these learnings, UX Writing began to be treated not only as a textual element of the interface, but as part of the food-safety experience itself within the product.
220.text: Instead of using overly technical or alarmist messages, Glútty’s communication sought to support the user during decision-making through:
221.text: more welcoming and objective language; progressive explanations; less ambiguity; contextualized risks; and reinforced transparency throughout navigation.
222.text: During this stage, it became clear that some writing decisions had a direct impact on the perceived trustworthiness of the experience. Small changes in tone, clarity and information hierarchy significantly changed how users interpreted the safety, adaptation and reliability of restaurants.
223.text: Writing was also used to reduce cognitive load at critical moments of the journey, especially during:
224.text: onboarding and setting up the food profile; interpreting ingredients and restrictions; reading community reviews; understanding safety levels; and viewing possible food risks.
225.text: Insert here images with examples of UX Writing applied to the interface.
226.text: Another important point identified during this stage was the need to avoid absolute promises of safety. Since the food context involves real health risks, the platform’s communication came to prioritize transparency and decision support instead of conveying false guarantees.
227.text: This direction directly influenced elements such as:
228.text: safety labels; food adaptation messages; community feedback; onboarding microcopy; empty states; notifications; and messages related to personalizing the experience.
229.text: Writing also helped reinforce emotional aspects of the experience, seeking to make the interface more welcoming for users who often live with fear, social limitation and emotional strain related to eating out.

231.text: More than guiding actions within the app, UX Writing began to work as a mechanism for building trust throughout the journey.
232.text: This stage helped consolidate one of the project’s main directions: at Glútty, communicating also means caring, reducing insecurity and supporting more conscious food decisions.
